newsitem.title: UK: Major squares up for new EU fight on working week.
newsitem.headline: Major squares up for new EU fight on working week.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major warned on Friday of another showdown with the European Union if a court ruling on the maximum working week goes against Britain.

Major, who is still at loggerheads with the EU over a ban on British beef imposed because of fears of mad cow disease, said he would demand to have the law overturned if the European Court of Justice ruled against Britain.
"If we lost that case, which I think would be outrageous, we would seek to have the European law changed," he told BBC television.
Britain is challenging a 1993 directive that would bar employees in many industries from working more than 48 hours a week.

Major reiterated his belief that the European Commission, the EU executive, was wrong to introduce the regulations as a health and safety measure and not as part of the bloc's Social Chapter on workplace standards.
Britain won an opt-out from the Social Chapter during negotiations on the 1991 Maastricht treaty on economic and political union.
"We believe it is wrong to try and impose it on the U.K.," Major said. "I have reached a decision at Maastricht that I now believe is being infringed."
The court is expected to give its verdict later this month. If past cases are a guide, it is likely to endorse a preliminary ruling in March that went against Britain.

If Britain loses, Major said, he would take his case to the intergovernmental conference (IGC) which is debating how to reform the institutions of the 15-nation bloc so it can expand to accommodate new members from eastern Europe.

Major, who would have the power to veto any reforms, said: "If that is the case I am going to seek to have the matter returned to what I thought I agreed some time ago, in the next IGC. We are going to have to reach agreement there, it is an important matter.

The opposition Labour Party, which has vowed to sign up to the Social Chapter if it wins the next general election, said it hoped Britain was not headed for total confrontation with the EU over a 48-hour week.

"I hope they don't reinforce Britain's reputation as being a one-country awkward squad, totally isolated in Europe. That would be a very expensive mistake for this country, and a very sad one," Labour's chief parliamentary manager, Donald Dewar, said.
Dewar noted the directive exempted certain occupations and would not prevent employees volunteering to work more than 48 hours a week. "It reinforces choice," he told a news conference.
